data.title: With nothing to lose, Republicans still put America last
data.description:
Last week, the Senate voted on a resolution would force the State Department to produce a report on Israeli violence in the West Bank. The legislation would require the State Department to report on human rights in countries receiving American security funds within 30 days. If the department fails to produce a report in time, those funds halt automatically.

West Bank violence is of particular interest to some lawmakers for good reason. For one, that violence has reached an “all-time high” which “threatens mass atrocities.” Second, the United States has the power to stop it. While West Bank attacks are typically committed by Israeli settlers, Israel’s government enables these crimes. It avoids confronting settlers as a matter of policy and even arms their attacks. That’s why Israeli human rights watchdog B’Tselem characterizes settler attacks as “state violence.” As its largest benefactor, the United States could pressure that state to shape up.

This is all the more pressing because Americans are increasingly the victims. Since 2022, at least nine U.S. citizens have been killed in the West Bank. None of the perpetrators have faced accountability. It’s a striking trend: a foreign government, funded and armed by the United States, killing Americans without repercussion. You’d think lawmakers would unanimously be desperate for answers. But you would be wrong.

The resolution failed on a 47-51 vote. Democrats, with the sole and unsurprising exception of Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, universally supported the resolution. All it would’ve taken was a few Republican votes to pass. The measure only got one: Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky. With the resolution’s fate resting in Republican hands, the conference closed ranks almost to a man.

It was a gut check for the GOP. The party of “America First” had a golden opportunity to affirm its patriotism. The resolution was their chance to show the world American lives take precedence over laundering a foreign country’s image. And it was a layup. The resolution simply required a report that, coming from the Trump State Department, probably would’ve been a whitewash anyway. It wouldn’t be some revelation that shattered Israel’s popularity or irreparably damaged the American-Israeli alliance. This was a freebie — a morally obvious and politically costless stand.

Domestically, it’s hard to imagine how anyone could object to seeking answers regarding American deaths abroad. Explaining to your constituents why you voted yes wouldn’t be hard. If anything, it’d be hard to explain voting no, which calls your loyalty to this country into question.

Yet Republicans voted no anyway. This wasn’t out of character; the GOP regularly undermines its own “America First” branding. It was nonetheless notable, though, for its nakedness. With other violations of “America First,” there is at least some deniability — however implausible. Take the ongoing war on Iran. Opponents have cast the administration’s ready willingness to bear the entanglement’s immense domestic costs as putting America last. But the administration and its supporters argue that this war is necessary for American security, which Iran threatens existentially. That’s wrong; but it’s a story. A shred of contestability can go a long way.

Similar mental gymnastics were at play when President Trump waived his aid pause for a $20-billion bailout of Argentina. The optics were undeniably poor: sending huge sums to keep afloat a fiscally reckless foreign government as Americans languish. But the administration had an answer. This too was “America First” — a strategic loan (not handout) to counter Chinese influence, maintaining American primacy in its “backyard.” Or, at least, that’s what they claimed. Feel free to dispute it. But there was some narrative that reconciled the move with the GOP’s nationalist marketing.

With the resolution on Israel, there simply isn’t one. Republicans are just nakedly taking the side of a foreign power. No “America First” story is even the least bit plausible here. It’s exactly what it seems.

Last week’s vote largely flew under the radar. But it was highly consequential for the conservative movement. It proved, beyond a shadow of a doubt, that their rallying cry is hollow. “America First” doesn’t denote any genuine commitment to prioritizing this land or its people. If it was even the least bit literal, the resolution would’ve passed resoundingly. But it didn’t. The pledge is remarkably devoid of content. Even when America First-ers have nothing to lose, they won’t abide by it. You often hear people critique the empty sloganeering of the left. But there is no slogan in United States politics more empty than “America First.” 

Elias Khoury is a University of Michigan law graduate and freelance writer based in Arlington, Virginia. He also holds a graduate degree in public policy from the London School of Economics.

data.title: White House on Trump purchasing SpaceX debt before space order: 'No conflicts of interest'
data.description:
The White House said on Friday there was no conflict of interest when President Trump’s accounts bought more than $1 million in SpaceX debt two days before he signed an executive order on space transportation policy.

The president’s financial disclosure for August, published Thursday, shows Trump’s accounts purchased between $1 million and $5 million in senior unsecured notes from Elon Musk’s aerospace and connectivity firm, Space Exploration Technologies Corp., on Aug. 18.

On Aug. 20, Trump signed a presidential memoranda to “reinvigorate America’s leadership in space transportation,” and allow for more than 1,000 launches and reentries on American land each year by 2030.

When asked about the purchase, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said “Trump’s stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions.”

“Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold,” Ingle continued. “All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers. There are no conflicts of interest.”

It is not clear who or what institution made the decision to purchase the SpaceX debt.

Trump has faced scrutiny in both his first and second White House terms for the blurring between his administration and family’s businesses. Trump’s investments and business assets are held in a trust managed by his children rather than divesting assets or placing them in a blind trust.

“All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000,” Ingle said.

More than 500 securities transactions were listed in the latest disclosure, including the purchase of Meta Platforms’ stock for between $5 and $25 million. A CNBC analysis of the August disclosure estimated the total purchases and sales listed was between $74.3 million and $273.3 million.

Musk’s SpaceX dominates the commercial space sector and has reportedly launched more satellites than the rest of humanity combined. Earlier this week, Trump awarded Musk and other tech executives the National Medal of Science at the White House’s “Science: A New Golden Age” summit.

Musk, who briefly worked as an advisor for Trump at the start of his second term, played a large role in the president’s 2024 reelection campaign. The tech billionaire was the president’s largest individual donor for his 2024 campaign.

Despite an explosive public feud last year, Trump and Musk have since mended fences publicly, with the tech executive appearing with the president at various events this year.

data.title: Mullin rails against Mamdani: 'His words are dangerous and incite hostility'
data.description:
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin bashed New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Friday for his response to a recent Immigration and Customs Enforcement(ICE) involved shooting in the city. 

Mullin said Mamdani’s public statements are dangerous and that he is performing “political theater.”

“I am speaking facts, the mayor speaks with political tone,” Mullin said at a press conference Friday. “His words are dangerous and incite hostility, it doesn’t help.”

ICE shot an undocumented immigrant — later identified as Oscar Belgal, a 28-year-old from the Dominican Republic —  in the neck Thursday while he was driving with five-year-old child in the car. Belgal, who has a criminal record, was taken to an area hospital and the child remains unharmed and with a family member. 

Mamdani railed against ICE at a press conference Thursday night and said there was no explanation for the tactics used. The mayor said he spoke with President Trump and Mullin Thursday night in an attempt to get Begal released, but that he was unsuccessful. 

Mullin said President Trump agreed to release Belgal to New York Police Department(NYPD) custody if they were willing to pursue charges against him, but that Mamdani did not agree. He said Belgal may have only been in the U.S. for the past three years, during which he participated in “extensive criminal activity.” 

Mamdani called for ICE to release body-cam footage of the incident. NYPD released body-cam footage from their officers in the moments after the shooting Friday.

Mullin went after the mayor for calling Belgal a New Yorker and criticized Mamdani’s statement that “ICE is rotten to the core.” Mamdani has called for the abolishment of ICE. 

“Really? The men and women of ICE each day are enforcing the laws that he refuses to enforce,” Mullin said. “We arrest thousands weekly that are criminals, going after the worst of the worst and he turns a blind eye to it.”

Mullin said ICE was serving a lawful order and that Belgal had evaded them once before. He said ICE was not aware that the child was in the car during the encounter, and that the officers involved will be put on administrative leave while they investigate the situation. 

The secretary said Belgal did know the child was there when he accelerated his car to a “high speed,” and that the public should blame him. 

“The public outcry should be also toward this criminal, this thug, this gang-banger, this possible murderer,” Mullin said. 

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Belgal pleaded guilty to grand larceny and that an investigation into the criminal sale of drugs involving Belgal is ongoing and had been taken over by federal agents.

data.title: When ICE hides detainees, constitutional rights go missing
data.description:
Thousands of people in ICE custody have been effectively “disappeared” by the U.S. government, according to new reporting by The Associated Press.  

The names of immigrant detainees with final orders of removal have vanished from the Online Detainee Locator System, a database that lets families and lawyers find out where detainees are.

Nearly 16,000 people booked into ICE detention in July were subject to final removal, the AP noted — more than one-third of the overall bookings. 

This policy of hiding the location of some detainees reflects the cruel and secretive nature of the administration’s immigration crackdown. It raises serious logistical and legal issues, and should be recognized for what it is: an assault on due process and constitutional rights.  

To be clear, this move does not apply to all detainees — just those with a final order of removal. A final order of removal is a document issued by an immigration judge that directs a non-citizen to leave the U.S.  

However, persons with final orders of removal may still have options to re-open their cases or file appeals. Some people with final orders are eligible for humanitarian relief under the United Nations Convention Against Torture, which prohibits sending people back to countries where they would face persecution or torture. Many people are issued final orders because they unintentionally missed a court date, or because a government notice was sent to the wrong address.  

That’s why the locator system is important. The system is a lifeline for detainees, their families, and their legal counsel. Families use the system to get in touch with their loved ones; immigration attorneys use it to set up meetings with their clients and gather evidence for cases.

As if it were not enough to wipe people’s names from the online locator, the Washington Post reports that immigration officials are now barred from revealing the locations of detainees to their relatives or attorneys over the phone. This puts the burden of communication on detainees. Yet it is not easy for people in detention to make phone calls to the outside. Calls are expensive, and often involve long lines and facility restrictions.

It is especially paramount that detainees are able to make contact, as ICE is constantly transfers people all around the country and even is carrying out illegal deportations.  

Removing people from the online locator system itself is likely illegal. Obstructing detainees from access to legal counsel violates their due process rights under the Fifth Amendment, because a lawyer cannot adequately represent their client if they don’t know where they are. Most critically, the move interferes with habeas corpus, a legal process that allows all people to challenge their detention in court. This mechanism is enshrined in the Constitution — and it is available to both citizens and non-citizens.  

Legal arguments aside, what reasonable person believes that government-enforced disappearances of prisoners is a good idea? This is a concept associated with authoritarian regimes like North Korea and the former Soviet Union. For Americans who worry about “the deep state,” this policy seems like a good example of it in action. 

In a statement, ICE said that detainees with final removal orders were being prioritized for deportation, even though ICE faces a “historic number of injunctions” from courts stopping individual removals. This answer is telling. As of May, federal judges have indeed ruled against the Trump administration in more than 20,000 ICE cases. But if the agency is facing so many court decisions blocking its actions, the solution is not to make detainees harder to trace. The solution is for ICE to reform its practices so that they comply with the law. 

Meanwhile, the stakes for people in immigration detention could not be higher. This year is on track for a record number of detainee deaths, and the administration has been sending detainees to remote third-world countries like Eswatini and Rwanda. The inability of a lawyer to reach a client in detention could have life-altering consequences. 

If pollsters are correct and Democrats regain control of Congress in the November midterms, lawmakers must ensure that the names of all immigrant detainees appear correctly in the online locator system. Lawmakers could also require that the locator stay updated in a timely manner and that lawyers be notified of detainee transfers. Government-sanctioned disappearances do not belong in a democracy. 

Raul A. Reyes is an immigration attorney and television commentator in New York City.

data.title: Grassley defends record after attacks from Democrats over Jack Smith treatment
data.description:
Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) defended his record after the committee’s Democrats called on the GOP side of the panel to apologize to former special counsel Jack Smith.

The letter from Grassley to Democrats makes little reference to the conduct that spurred a prevoius letter from ranking member Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) – a line of questioning from Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Iowa) in which he accused Smith of being present at a basketball game in Atlanta in an effort to tie the prosecutor to follow President Trump investigator Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis (D).

Smith was not at an Atlanta Hawks game in that city on the night in question, but instead was in Maryland to see the women’s Iowa Hawkeyes play.

In Thursday’s letter, Democrats also demanded that Grassley turn over the texts that Schmitt used as the basis for his questions, some of which were flashed during the healing with Smith, citing the need to do so under committee rules.

“Contrary to your misguided statement, the major embarrassment of the hearing was Democrats falling over themselves defending unlawful and unconstitutional actions by Jack Smith,” Grassley wrote in his letter.

The four-page letter to Durbin lays out a number of grievances Grassley has with committee Democrats, accusing them of defending what he sees as improper prosecutorial conduct with Smith as well as a failure by Democrats to always be transparent with the other side.

Grassley also faults Smith for withholding certain records – though it would be up to the Justice Department to release those files. That includes what he called 800 pages of emails “at the center mass of this Committee’s investigation.”

Grassley has said much of the information he has received on Smith’s investigations have come from whistleblowers, not directly in Justice Department disclosures.

He said, however, he would not yet be turning those over to Democrats, citing the need to protect his sources from retaliation. 

“Ultimately, the public still awaits a full accounting of Jack Smith and his Special Counsel staff’s conduct. The investigation is active, the hearing is not the end of my work, and therefore some records will not be shared with you until a later date. But, rest assured, as I have in the past, you will be given access to those records, including next week when our respective staff meet. 

The letter underscores tensions on a committee that has a long history of working in a bipartisan fashion and traditionally has had good relationships at the staff level as well.

Grassley said both sides are set to meet next week.

In a statement, Durbin’s team said they have still yet to receive the records they demanded.

“Chairman Grassley’s letter spends four pages spinning conspiracy theories without ever addressing the fact that Republicans continue to violate Senate Rules by withholding from Democrats the documents that were the basis for the false accusations of perjury against Jack Smith,” a Durbin spokesperson said.

“Republicans remain laser focused on attacking Mr. Smith because they don’t want to talk about President Trump’s disgraceful and un-American crimes that Mr. Smith was investigating.”

data.title: Live updates: Trump sets up commission to investigate Lisa Cook
data.description:
President Trump set in motion an administrative panel Friday to investigate mortgage fraud allegations against Federal Reserve board of governors member Lisa Cook in his latest effort to fire her.

The inquiry will include a hearing at the White House on Nov. 5 that Cook “shall” attend to answer questions from the committee, Trump said in a written memo.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) reacted angrily toward the shooting of an immigrant by a federal officer while a child was present Thursday.

“There is no justification for what we have seen today,” Mamdani said. The mayor added that he spent two hours Thursday night pressing Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to release the wounded man.

Trump is holding a rally in upstate New York on Friday after focusing his crunch-time campaign blitz for GOP candidates in red states.

He will stump in Syracuse, N.Y., to give a last-minute boost to Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman — whom nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) gave a 10 percent chance of winning as of Thursday night.

Within the past week, the president has made stops in Texas, Oklahoma, Alabama and Nebraska — all of which he claimed in 2024. This weekend, he’ll be in Tennessee and Alabama, with a rally in Alaska next week.

Vice President Vance is rallying voters in Lima, Ohio. While DDHQ ranks Ohio’s 4th Congressional District, home to Lima, a “safe” Republican victory, the state’s Senate race is much tighter — with former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) narrowly leading his GOP opponent, incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R) as of late September.

Follow live below.

data.title: Israel calls Navi Pillay's win a 'grotesque weaponization' of Nobel Peace Prize
data.description:
Israel’s Foreign Ministry on Friday fumed over what it described as the “grotesque weaponization” of the Nobel Peace Prize after the award was won by former International Criminal Court (ICC) judge Navanethem Pillay.

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner. Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonization of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes,” the Israeli Foreign Ministry wrote on social media. “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.”

Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her contributions to enlarging the scope and impact of international law. She recently oversaw a United Nations report that concluded that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. 

The September report by a team of independent experts commissioned by the U.N. Human Rights Council concluded “the Israeli authorities and Israeli security forces have the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.”

“The Commission finds that Israel is responsible for the commission of genocide in Gaza,” Pillay said in a press release.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Natanyahu similarly criticzed Pillay receivving the prize in a post on social media, saying the Nobel Peace Prize committee “has lost its moral compass.” 

“It has awarded its highest honor to a bigot who built her career around inventing and propagating blood libels against the one and only Jewish state,” he added.

Netanyahu also claimed that Pillay’s “proudest achievement was to legitimize a corrupt prosecutor,” referring to former ICC chief prosecutor Karim Khan.

Khan was removed from his post after sexual misconduct allegations from a female aide surfaced. The court’s 125 member states voted to remove Khan but the allegations against the former chief prosecutor became entwined with the court’s investigation into the war in Gaza, experts said at the time, according to the Associated Press.

Hours after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded, the U.S. imposed sanctions against the ICC which has attempted to pursue war crimes cases against the Trump administration, American servicemembers and Israel.

ICC President Tomoko Akane, who was sanctioned by the Trump administration in August, stated the court would continue to investigate and prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity.

data.title: Read Guilfoyle's texts to GOP donor Deters: 'You'll literally cost me my ambassadorship'
data.description:
Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece and former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., is under new scrutiny for allegedly requesting a direct deposit of $100,000 from a MAGA donor to clear her credit card debt ahead of her Senate confirmation hearing. 

In text messages obtained by NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network, Guilfoyle appears to plead with Eric Deters, a former lawyer and Kentucky congressional candidate, to send money directly to her American Express account so it can’t be tracked.

“Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” Guilfoyle wrote in one message to the GOP donor dated July 3, 2025, six days before her confirmation hearing.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the texts, sent via Signal, late Wednesday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio declined to comment on the scandal when pressed by reporters on Thursday.

NewsNation reached out to Guilfoyle’s lawyers on Thursday for comment.

One of her lawyers told The Journal she “disputed the authenticity of the messages but declined to provide specifics.” Jesse Binnall told The Journal that Guilfoyle was owed a balance related to speaking events, which Deters disputed.

Read some of the key text messages between Guilfoyle and Deters:

In Signal messages that Deters told NewsNation were exchanged in the weeks before Guilfoyle’s confirmation hearing, she urged him not to tell people about their “arrangement” and warned he could “literally cost me my ambassadorship.”

Deters pressed Guilfoyle throughout their exchanges to help him score interviews on former Fox News host Tucker Carlson’s show and Donald Trump Jr.’s podcast as part of his efforts to push for the extradition of an Ohio doctor who had fled to Pakistan after being charged with defrauding insurers by performing unnecessary spinal surgeries.

He also asked her to connect him with then-Attorney General Pam Bondi and FBI Director Kash Patel in relation to the case. And he pushed for access to Billy Long, who was serving as the commissioner of the Internal Revenue Service at the time, to discuss a tax-related matter, and with Kid Rock to share a song he wrote called “Kentucky Outlaw.”

Guilfoyle repeatedly stressed that she wanted to keep the conversations between herself and Deters private — and communicate through phone calls.

A call log shared with NewsNation showed eight phone conversations between the pair between June and early July 2025. The pair also exchanged voice note recordings at times.

Deters pledged his support for Guilfoyle in several messages, writing in a Signal exchange on June 11, 2025, that she could “count” on him in her future role as ambassador. Guilfoyle welcomed his assistance and said she would host him in Greece as her “special guest.”

But Guilfoyle grew increasingly frustrated with Deters for putting things in writing.

In a letter in late June, attached as a PDF in the chat, Deters wrote he “generously offered” her $1 million if she “got me on Tucker” and had already paid her $300,000 over the years. He also complained that Guilfoyle had not connected him with neither Bondi nor Long.

“As of this memo, I have not received one favor,” he wrote. “I am not naive or a sucker. I need results. No results. No need for me to pay.”

Guilfoyle replied, urging him to “stop papering all these things.”

On July 2, Guilfoyle sent another plea for Deters to “get this done for me today.”

In response to that message, Deters wrote that he’s “trying [to] figure something out.” The next day, Guilfoyle appeared to send specific instructions for where to send money.

Deters responded with another letter on July 7, telling Guilfoyle, “I can’t do this without getting a divorce.”

“Just do the best you can. I wish you luck on your confirmation and appreciate your help,” he adds, signing the letter “Jason Statham,” a reference to his action-movie-like driving during one of her visits to Kentucky.

In response, Guilfoyle called the letter “upsetting” and again told Deters he should have called.

NewsNation’s Sam Marks contributed reporting.

data.title: Watch live: Vance rallies home state voters as Ohio Senate race tightens
data.description:
Vice President Vance is returning to his home state Friday to rally voters as Republican Sen. Jon Husted looks to fend off a familiar Democratic challenger to maintain his seat in the upper chamber.

Vance will headline the campaign event in Lima, Ohio, as the GOP looks to boost turnout with the midterms now less than a month away. The party is also fighting to keep its control of Congress next year.

Former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) is hoping to flip the seat, which the vice president once held, for Democrats.

President Trump, who has also ramped up his campaign efforts in recent weeks, will visit the state on Monday. Trump and Vance are also seeking to grow support for Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy.

The event is scheduled to begin at 1:30 p.m. EDT.

data.title: To strengthen child welfare and keep families together, we need structural change
data.description:
For decades, policymakers have built federal child welfare policy brick by brick, relying on outdated assumptions about what the government should do when children and families struggle. They have designed programs and prescribed resources, while rigid funding structures have bound these layers together.

Over time, this structure has hardened in place, despite overwhelming data that challenges the child welfare financing institution and its corresponding incentives. Today, more than 2 million American families are investigated by Child Protective Services each year.

In 84 percent of those cases, there is no substantiated finding of abuse or neglect. Yet every year, approximately 175,000 children enter foster care, despite decades of outcomes that show the harm the intervention itself causes, and even when we now know there is no association between foster care entries and child maltreatment fatalities. 

For Nate Bustamente, family separation was an inescapable throughline in his life. Bustamente entered foster care as a child, and years later, after becoming a parent himself, he and his wife faced a child welfare case involving their own children. He worked long hours to meet the requirements imposed on his family while navigating the possibility of losing his children. After a second removal, the state pursued termination of his and his wife’s parental rights. Despite months of compliance, they still had to defend their right to remain a family in court.

Bustamente credits his attorney and the family-time supervisor who observed his family’s visits with helping the court understand what was happening in their lives. The judge denied the termination petition, and the case eventually closed. Reflecting on that moment, Bustamente described how he could finally breathe without carrying the weight of what might happen to his family — an experience facing too many families caught in the crosshairs of an unforgiving system.

United Family Advocates, a bipartisan group of child welfare advocates, attorneys, researchers and nonprofit leaders, recently released a framework to shed light on how federal child welfare financing is structured in ways that too often make family separations like Bustamente’s the path of least resistance, when it should be the last resort. 

As federal policymakers increasingly examine whether existing child welfare funding mechanisms adequately support child safety, family stability, and responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars, it is clear that the patchwork that created the fundamental financing structure we have today needs significant reform. The current structure is an entitlement program, and functions as a $10 billion entitlement to separate families.

States need greater flexibility to invest in the community-based supports families actually need to address housing, food, mental health, substance use, or other challenges, while preserving a clear role for protecting children facing imminent danger. Funding should also include resources families can access without having to enter the child welfare system, and access to high-quality legal representation to help ensure families have fair processes when such highly consequential decisions about their children and family are being made.

Federal policymakers have important debates ahead of them about what proportion of federal resources should go toward maintaining a system that responds to family crises versus building the infrastructure that helps families avoid those crises in the first place. 

For Bustamente, a continuum of community support to address his family’s needs without making separation the default response could have changed the trajectory of his life. His question is simple: How many more families have to go through what he went through? The constant fear and the lost time with his children are not inevitable.

For decades, policymakers have added brick after brick to sustain a system that relies on separation as its primary intervention. It is time to stop reinforcing the status quo and start rebuilding a foundation that gives families the support they need before crisis becomes separation.

Joanna Lack is executive director of United Family Advocates.
